candidate_payload.early_body_text: letter to the editor the relationship between cortical and spinal hyperexcitability and clinical disease severity in stiff-man syndrome keywords: stiff-man syndrome cortical hyperexcitability spinal hyperexcitability transcranial magnetic stimulation threshold tracking technique 1. introduction stiff-man syndrome (sms) is an autoimmune disorder charac- terised by ﬂuctuating muscular rigidity and spasms, most promi- nent in axial and proximal limb muscles usually in a symmetric manner. serum anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (gad) antibody is present in 60 –80% of patients and there is evidence of both cortical and spinal hyperexcitability, as detected by paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (tms) and exteroceptive reﬂexes, respectively [1]. signi ﬁcantly, cortical hyperexcitability has been shown to correlate with csf anti-gad antibody level [2], suggesting that anti-gad antibodies underlie the cortical hyperexcitability, but the relationship between cortical and spinal hyperexcitability and their role in the development of clinical features remain obscure. therefore, the present study assessed the relationship between cortical and spinal hyperexcitability, and the relationship between either cortical or spinal hyperexcit- ability and clinical features of sms. 2. methods studies were undertaken in 5 patients with sms (1 male, 4 females, mean age 57.8 years, age range 26–83). the diagnosis of sms was based on a typical presenta- tion with back pain, stiffness and stimulus-induced spasms in 4/5 and stiff limb syndrome subsequently generalising in 1 patient, together with supportive investi- gations including positive anti-gad antibodies and exteroceptive reﬂexes at presen- tation in all patients. at the time of testing, all patients exhibited stable disease and their therapy had not been changed for at least 3 months. regular medications included benzodiazepines that were not discontinued for the study. all patients gave informed consent to the procedures, which were approved by the sydney western area health service human research ethics committee. all patients were clinically staged using the distribution-of-stiffness and height- ened sensitivity scales based on reported symptoms in the preceding week, as previ- ously described by dalakas et al. [3]. anti-gad antibody levels were measured at the same visit using gad65 anti- body elisa kit (rsr ltd, cardiff, uk). the results are reported in manufacturer’s units per millilitre. cortical excitability studies were undertaken using the paired-pulse threshold tracking tms with a 90 mm circular coil as previously reported. brie ﬂy, the motor evoked potential (mep) amplitude, recorded over the right abductor pollicis brevis, was ﬁxed and changes in the test stimulus intensity required to generate a target response of 0.2 mv ( /c6 20%), when preceded by sub-threshold conditioning stimuli, were measured. resting motor threshold (rmt) was de ﬁned as the stimulus inten- sity required to maintain this target mep response. short interval intracortical inhi- bition (sici) and intracortical facilitation (icf) were measured according to a previously devised protocol [4]. cortical silent period (csp) duration was recorded with magnetic stimulus intensity set to 140% rmt. spinal excitability was assessed with exteroceptive re ﬂexes using a modi ﬁed technique of meinck et al. [5]. brieﬂy, a train of 6 square wave pulses of 0.5 ms dura- tion and 1.5 –2.0 times the motor threshold (as detected by muscle twitch) were delivered at 200 hz to the median nerve at the wrist just proximal to the wrist crease and surface electromyographic recordings were obtained over the sternocleidomas- toid, paraspinals at c7, t4, t12, l4, and rectus femoris muscles. 3. statistics cortical excitability in sms patients was compared to 61 healthy controls. student t-test test was used to compare mean differences and correlations between excitability indices and clinical scales were analysed by pearson ’s rank test. results are expressed as mean /c6 standard error of the mean. 4. results the clinical and laboratory characteristics of the 5 sms patients are outlined in table 1. the mean disease severity score was 5.8 (range: 0 –12), indicating a mild-to-moderate level of disease activity. all patients tested positive for anti-gad antibodies and the mean anti-gad antibody level was 1,248,974 u/ml (normal <10 u/ml). sici and csp duration were signi ﬁcantly reduced in sms patients while icf was increased ( fig. 1). in contrast, extero- ceptive re ﬂexes were abnormal at presentation but absent in all but one patient at the time of this study. there was no signi ﬁcant correlation between sici and the heightened sensitivity ( r ¼ 0.31, p ¼ 0.61) or distribution of stiffness ( r ¼ 0.31, p ¼ 0.62). there was no signi ﬁcant correlation between sici ( r ¼ 0.22, p ¼ 0.99), icf ( r ¼/c0 0.5, p ¼ 0.39) or csp ( r ¼/c0 0.154, p ¼ 0.80) and serum anti-gad antibody levels. assessment of csf anti-gad antibodies
